sentences.text: The species Dsungaripterus weii is known to have had a wingspan ranging from 2 to 3.5 meters.
This large pterosaur possessed a head and neck size comparable to a human arm.
Its robust skeleton featured thick bone walls, suggesting the animal spent most of its time on the ground.
The skull measured over 46 cm in length and featured a low bone crest extending from the skull base to the middle of the beak.
The genus Dsungaripterus was first described in 1964 by the paleontologist Yang Zhongjian.
Researchers commonly interpret Dsungaripterus as a durophagous, or shell-crushing, pterosaur that may have also eaten fish.
The front part of its jaws lacked teeth and was likely used to extract prey from rock cracks or sandy, muddy environments.
Flat, knobbly teeth at the back of its jaws were adapted for crushing the shells of hard objects like shellfish.
Yang classified Dsungaripterus as a member of the family Dsungaripteridae.
Fossils of Dsungaripterus are found in the Wuerho Pterosaur Fauna group within the Junggar Basin of China.
The time range for Dsungaripterus is estimated from the Valanginian to the Barremian, between 137.05 and 121.4 million years ago.
While some deposits containing Dsungaripterus fossils date to the middle Valanginian, the exact age range of these layers remains uncertain.
A 2019 study by Kellner and colleagues recovered Dsungaripterus outside the Azhdarchoidea, placing it within Tapejaroidea as a sister taxon to Noripterus.
